title: Rav Avira (I)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was a native of the Land of Israel, a disciple of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, as Hyman says we always find Rav Avira expounding, sometimes in the name of Rabbi Ami and sometimes in the name of Rabbi Assi: in Berakhot 20b; Pesachim 109b; Gittin 7a; Sotah 4b; Chullin 84b.

And we find in Sukkah 52a that Rav Avira, or perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, expounded: The evil inclination has seven names. And in Pesachim 110b he said: Bowls and loaves are not subject to the concern of pairs.
And in Ketubot 102a: Rabbi Chelbo and Rabbi Avira and Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina happened to come to a certain place; the following year Rabbi Elazar happened to come there, etc.

In Abaye’s time he came to Babylonia. In Chullin 51a, Rav Safra told Abaye, “Look at this rabbinic scholar who has come from the West and says, ‘My name is Rav Avira.’” Abaye sent for him, but he would not come; Abaye therefore went to him. He told Abaye, “I served as the attendant who assembled and dismissed the students before Rabbi Rabbah.” (Rashi identifies Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; Hyman says this should undoubtedly be Rabbi Yehuda Nesia. He prefers the interpretation in Yuchasin, first essay, entry Rabbi: Rabbi Yochanan, who was called Rabbi Rabbah. Although Rav Avira was a student of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, Hyman explains that this was still during Rabbi Yochanan’s lifetime.)

notes.text: Rashi on Chullin51a explains maftir kenesiyyot as assembling and dismissing students from the study house; it is not a comparison of his stature with Rabbi Rabbah or a haftarah-reading statement. Rashi’s Yehuda HaNasi identification and Hyman’s alternatives Yehuda Nesia/Yochanan remain distinct, attributed interpretations.

The consulted Rashi Chullin 51a explains the assembly-and-dismissal role and identifies Rabbi Rabbah as Yehudah HaNasi. Hyman’s undoubtedly-Yehudah-Nesia emendation and preference for Yuchasin’s Yochanan identification remain distinct attributed interpretations. His source-wide “always” assertion is retained without treating the selected passages as exhaustive proof.
